strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: producing voxel-level natural-language interpretations of human visual cortex responses.
LaVCa is a sensible modular pipeline that can use modern multimodal and language models without task-specific captioner training.
Held-out correlations improve consistently over the authors' BrainSCUBA reimplementation across four NSD subjects, multiple voxel-count thresholds, and both sentence- and image-mediated evaluations.
The paper includes useful hyperparameter ablations, shuffled-caption controls, ROI analyses, and extensive qualitative visualizations.
The privacy implications of increasingly detailed brain interpretation are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The evaluation is heavily model-mediated and partly circular. LaVCa is constructed from CLIP features, while image-level evaluation uses generated images embedded by the same CLIP vision model; sentence-level evaluation similarly relies on another pretrained language embedding model. These tests do not establish that the captions are faithful or useful to humans.

No human or neuroscientist evaluation measures caption correctness, specificity, interpretability, or hallucination. Numerous displayed captions are ungrammatical or combine unsupported concepts, substantially weakening the central interpretability claim.

The diversity metrics are confounded by caption length, verbosity, and hallucination. Larger vocabulary, embedding variance, and more PCA dimensions need not represent meaningful neural selectivity; they can instead reflect noisier generations.

The claim that individual voxels simultaneously encode multiple distinct concepts is not supported by the experiments. The method explicitly asks an LLM for multiple concepts and composes them into one sentence, so multi-concept outputs may be artifacts of the pipeline rather than properties of the voxel.

The comparison is limited primarily to one independently reimplemented baseline whose training procedure and image pool differ from the original BrainSCUBA system. Stronger simple and modern baselines, controlled for caption length and language-model capacity, are missing.

Statistical inference is inadequately specified and potentially pseudoreplicated: paired tests appear to treat thousands of spatially dependent voxels as samples, while only four subjects are studied. Exact tests, effect-size uncertainty, correction scope, and subject-level inference are not reported.
Hyperparameter configurations appear to be compared using test accuracy, creating a risk that the final setting is test-selected. A validation split or nested selection protocol is needed.

Important reproducibility details are absent, including the keyword-filtering threshold, ridge-selection procedure, random seeds, complete generation settings, and a code release. Dependence on a proprietary API further limits exact reproduction.

The incremental combination of optimal-image retrieval, MLLM captioning, LLM keyword extraction, and an existing sentence composer is technically plausible, but the evidence is insufficient for the paper's stronger neuroscientific conclusions.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and important problem: producing voxel-level natural-language descriptions of selectivity in the human visual cortex.
LaVCa is a coherent modular pipeline that combines encoding models, large-scale image retrieval, multimodal captioning, keyword extraction, and constrained sentence generation.
Experiments use a substantial public fMRI dataset, evaluate four subjects, report both text- and image-based activity-prediction metrics, and include several hyperparameter ablations.
LaVCa consistently improves average held-out prediction correlations over the authors' BrainSCUBA implementation, although the absolute gains are modest.
weaknesses: The evaluation is substantially entangled with the construction pipeline. CLIP features are used to train the encoding model, retrieve images, filter keywords, guide sentence composition, and evaluate generated images. Consequently, improved CLIP-space consistency does not independently establish that the captions faithfully describe biological voxel selectivity.

There is no human evaluation of caption correctness or interpretability. This is especially problematic because many displayed LaVCa captions are ungrammatical, hallucinatory, or semantically incoherent. Proxy correlations alone do not support the paper's strong interpretability claims.

The comparison against BrainSCUBA is not definitive: the authors reimplemented it without public reference code and changed its optimization procedure and image corpus. Only one substantive prior method is compared, with insufficient strong simple baselines in the principal evaluation.

The diversity metrics are weak evidence of meaningful detail. Vocabulary size, sentence length, embedding variance, and the number of PCA components can all increase merely through verbosity, noise, or hallucination; they do not demonstrate accurate or useful semantic diversity, and the comparisons are not controlled for caption length.

The statistical analysis appears to treat thousands of spatially correlated voxels as independent observations in a paired t-test, despite having only four subjects. Subject-level inference, confidence intervals on improvements, and appropriate hierarchical or permutation tests are missing.

Hyperparameters are compared using test-set accuracy, with no clearly identified validation set, creating a risk of test-set selection bias. Important details such as ridge-parameter selection, random seeds, stochastic image-generation handling, and full end-to-end reproducibility are also incomplete.

The ROI-shuffling experiment does not establish fine-grained functional differentiation: shuffling disrupts voxel-specific matching, reliability, and spatial structure even when captions share the same broad category. Stronger controls are needed to separate genuine semantic specialization from voxel-specific noise and encoding-model variation.

The claim that individual voxels simultaneously represent multiple distinct concepts is not justified. fMRI voxels aggregate many neural populations, natural-image concepts are correlated, and the sentence composer is explicitly designed to merge multiple retrieved keywords; multi-concept generated captions therefore cannot establish biological multiplexing.

The study is limited to four selected NSD participants and lacks replication on another dataset, evaluation of cross-subject stability, or tests of whether the inferred selectivity generalizes beyond the same captioned natural-image distribution.

Overall, the method is technically plausible and the empirical improvements are consistent, but the evaluation does not validate the central scientific claims about faithful, fine-grained voxel interpretation strongly enough for a top-tier acceptance.

The empirical improvements over the authors' BrainSCUBA implementation are consistent across all four NSD participants, multiple voxel-selection thresholds, and both sentence- and image-level prediction metrics.
The paper includes useful ablations of the number of optimal images, number of extracted concepts, keyword extractor, and BrainSCUBA temperature, alongside a shuffled-caption control.

The comparison with concatenated optimal-image captions demonstrates an appealing accuracy-versus-conciseness tradeoff, and the ROI visualizations provide potentially useful exploratory tools for neuroscience.
The manuscript is generally well organized, documents model checkpoints and prompts, discusses privacy concerns, and acknowledges limitations in capturing local visual features.
weaknesses: The central interpretability claim is not validated by human raters or neuroscience experts. Several showcased captions are grammatically poor, hallucinatory, or combine seemingly unrelated concepts, making automated prediction scores insufficient evidence that the descriptions are genuinely accurate and interpretable.

The evaluation is strongly coupled to the construction pipeline: CLIP features define the encoding weights and optimal images, CLIP is used again for keyword filtering and sentence composition, and CLIP-based features underlie image-level evaluation. Although held-out brain responses provide some protection against direct circularity, evaluation with independent visual and language models is needed.

The principal comparison is against an in-house reconstruction of BrainSCUBA whose training procedure and source image pool differ from the original method. Without released code, validation against reported results, or additional strong captioning and concept-discovery baselines, the size of the claimed methodological advantage remains uncertain.

The statistical treatment is weak. Paired tests over thousands of spatially correlated voxels risk pseudoreplication, while only four participants are available. Subject-level or hierarchical inference, spatial/block bootstrapping, effect-size uncertainty, and clearer multiple-comparison handling are needed.

The diversity metrics largely reward verbosity and lexical variety: vocabulary size, sentence length, embedding variance, and PCA dimensionality do not establish semantic correctness or useful functional differentiation. Length-matched controls and human semantic judgments would make these results more convincing.

Claims that individual voxels encode multiple distinct concepts and that ROI results reveal fine-grained functional specialization are stronger than the evidence supports. An fMRI voxel aggregates many neurons, and multi-concept captions may arise from dataset co-occurrence, retrieval noise, or LLM composition rather than genuine conjunctive selectivity.

Reproducibility is limited by reliance on a proprietary GPT-4o API and the apparent absence of a clear code and generated-caption release statement. Overall, the method is promising and the results are encouraging, but these evaluation and validation gaps place it slightly below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: producing interpretable, voxel-specific descriptions of visual selectivity rather than only accurate but opaque encoding models.
The modular pipeline—optimal-image retrieval, multimodal captioning, keyword extraction/filtering, and sentence composition—is intuitive and potentially useful.
Experiments use held-out responses from four NSD participants, cover multiple visual ROIs, and include an additional BOLD5000 analysis.
The paper provides useful ablations over vision-language backbones, captioners, keyword-extraction models, prompts, numbers of images and keywords, and sentence-similarity models.
The alternative image-level evaluation, caption-length comparison, checkpoint details, and compute reporting are valuable attempts to assess robustness and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The evaluation is substantially entangled with the construction objective. CLIP features determine encoding weights, optimal images, keyword filtering, and sentence composition, while the image-level evaluation again uses CLIP after generating an image from the caption. This shared representation can reward alignment with the pipeline rather than faithful characterization of neural selectivity; the image-level result therefore does not constitute a sufficiently independent validation.

The main comparison is against an in-house BrainSCUBA reimplementation that changes both its training procedure and candidate-image corpus. Without the released implementation, matching reported performance, or additional strong baselines such as direct LLM set summarization and other neuron-description methods, it is difficult to attribute the gain to LaVCa rather than implementation choices.

The biological conclusions are much stronger than the evidence. Lower performance after shuffling captions within an ROI establishes voxel specificity, not previously unknown representational diversity. Likewise, forcing captions to incorporate several keywords and then counting how many arbitrary k-means noun clusters they span does not demonstrate that individual voxels genuinely encode multiple concepts.

The diversity metrics are heavily confounded by verbosity and model vocabulary. LaVCa captions are almost twice as long as BrainSCUBA captions, making larger vocabulary, greater word-embedding variance, and more occupied PCA dimensions expected. No human evaluation measures caption correctness, coherence, specificity, or usefulness, and several displayed LaVCa examples are ungrammatical or hallucinated.

Statistical testing is inadequate for the central method comparison. Paired tests over thousands of spatially correlated voxels risk pseudoreplication, whereas there are only four NSD participants. The paper does not report subject-level uncertainty, effect sizes, corrected tests across the many comparisons, or a hierarchical/spatially aware analysis. Pooling permutation correlations across voxels can also be invalid when voxel-specific null distributions differ.

The BOLD5000 experiment demonstrates nonzero performance but provides no comparison with BrainSCUBA or other baselines, so it does not establish that LaVCa's claimed advantage generalizes across datasets. Details needed to rule out image/repetition leakage and explain the COCO-category sensitivity analysis are also unclear.

Several key design choices are arbitrary or insufficiently justified, including five keywords, six noun clusters, UMAP-derived qualitative clusters, softmax filtering, and selecting the top 5,000 voxels. Although some sensitivity analyses are given, they do not validate the downstream neuroscientific interpretations.

Reproducibility remains limited: the stated public code location is blank in the manuscript, the method depends on a proprietary versioned API, and some terminology is confusing—for example, the nearly identical 'voxel-wise versus shared weights' ridge variants are not defined clearly enough to reproduce.

Overall, the work presents a plausible engineering extension with encouraging predictive results, but the circular evaluation, baseline uncertainty, problematic statistics, and unsupported claims about multi-concept neural representation are major issues for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and challenging problem: producing open-ended, voxel-level interpretations of human visual cortex responses.
LaVCa is a coherent modular pipeline that combines encoding models, large-scale optimal-image retrieval, multimodal captioning, keyword extraction, and sentence composition.

The empirical study is extensive, covering four NSD subjects, a secondary BOLD5000 analysis, sentence- and image-level metrics, multiple voxel-selection thresholds, and numerous component and hyperparameter ablations.

Results consistently improve over the authors’ BrainSCUBA implementation across NSD subjects, with held-out test responses used for evaluation. The appendix also reports checkpoints, prompts, computational costs, and several qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The evaluation is substantially entangled with the pipeline. CLIP representations are used to learn encoding weights, retrieve optimal images, filter keywords, guide sentence composition, and—after caption-to-image generation—evaluate image-level similarity. This shared model geometry can reward captions that reconstruct the CLIP encoding model rather than faithfully explain biological selectivity. The image-level experiment therefore does not constitute a sufficiently independent validation.

The baseline comparison is not definitive. BrainSCUBA is an in-house reimplementation that changes both its image corpus and encoding-model training, while the official implementation is not evaluated. SASC is discussed but omitted, and there is no competitive length- or information-matched LLM summarization baseline. LaVCa’s longer, five-concept output has an inherent advantage over BrainSCUBA’s short caption.

Interpretability and caption quality are not evaluated by humans or neuroscience experts. Several showcased LaVCa captions are conspicuously incoherent or hallucinated, such as combinations involving food packaging, animals, desserts, and unrelated objects. Sentence-embedding correlation does not establish that such captions are understandable, faithful explanations.

The diversity evidence is highly confounded. Vocabulary size and Word2Vec variance mechanically increase with caption length and verbosity. More importantly, the prompt explicitly requests five mutually distinct concepts; subsequently finding that captions contain nouns from multiple clusters is therefore partly a consequence of the generation procedure, not evidence that individual voxels biologically encode multiple concepts.

The strong neuroscience conclusions are unsupported. Within-ROI caption shuffling only shows that the pipeline assigns different captions to voxels; it does not validate those concepts or overturn assumptions about functional specialization. Category-selective regions are not generally assumed to encode only one category, and the reported word clouds, UMAP plots, generated images, and modest cross-subject similarities cannot establish new cortical organization.

Statistical reporting is insufficient for the claimed superiority. The paper reports paired t-tests without clearly defining the independent unit, despite strong spatial dependence among thousands of voxels and only four NSD subjects. It gives no subject-level confidence interval or robust hierarchical inference for method comparisons. The pooled permutation-null construction and subsequent voxel-wise FDR analysis also require stronger justification.

The BOLD5000 extension lacks comparison against BrainSCUBA or other baselines and supports cross-dataset reproducibility mainly through qualitative word-cloud correspondences. Evaluation is restricted to COCO trials, further limiting the generalization claim.

The technical novelty is moderate: the main contribution is a composition of existing retrieval, captioning, LLM summarization, filtering, and MeaCap components. Given the evaluation circularity and lack of independent semantic validation, the incremental construction is not yet supported as a reliable scientific measurement tool.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the manuscript’s source-code URL is blank, the pipeline depends on a proprietary versioned API, and full processing reportedly requires roughly 83 GPU-hours per subject on eight A100 GPUs.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and challenging problem: producing fine-grained, natural-language interpretations of voxel selectivity rather than relying on coarse predefined semantic categories.

LaVCa is a clear and modular pipeline that separates optimal-image retrieval, image captioning, keyword extraction, filtering, and sentence composition. This makes the approach flexible across vision-language and language-model backbones.

The empirical study is extensive. It covers four NSD subjects, sentence- and image-level evaluations, several voxel-selection thresholds, cortical and ROI analyses, numerous component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and an additional BOLD5000 experiment.

The reported improvements over the implemented BrainSCUBA baseline are consistent across subjects and both principal evaluation modalities. The concise-caption versus concatenation comparison also demonstrates a useful accuracy–length tradeoff.
The appendix provides substantial implementation detail, prompts, model checkpoints, computational costs, qualitative examples, and hyperparameter studies.
weaknesses: The evaluation is heavily mediated by pretrained models that also construct the explanations. CLIP features define the encoding model, retrieve optimal images, filter keywords, and score candidates; image-level evaluation again uses CLIP after generating an image from the caption. Although correlations are computed against held-out fMRI responses, this shared representational machinery makes the results partly a test of consistency with the chosen model ecosystem rather than independent evidence of faithful voxel interpretation.

There is no human evaluation of caption correctness, coherence, or usefulness. This is important because many displayed LaVCa captions are grammatically awkward or semantically implausible, despite the paper's claim that the method produces highly interpretable descriptions.

The comparison to prior work is narrow and potentially fragile. BrainSCUBA is an in-house reimplementation that changes its image pool and encoding-model training, while SASC and other plausible language-based interpretation baselines are not evaluated. Consequently, the superiority claim over existing approaches is not fully established.

The neuroscience conclusions are overstated. Greater vocabulary, within-ROI shuffling effects, and noun clusters derived from generated captions do not by themselves demonstrate that individual voxels encode multiple distinct concepts or overturn established accounts of category-selective cortex. A voxel aggregates many neurons, and the observed diversity may arise from the caption-generation pipeline, correlated visual features, or noise.

The diversity metrics are confounded by caption length and lexical verbosity: longer captions almost mechanically have larger vocabularies and can occupy more variable embedding space. More diversity is not necessarily more faithful information, and no precision or hallucination analysis is provided.

Statistical inference treats thousands of spatially correlated voxels as paired samples, while the central biological conclusions are based on only four NSD subjects. Subject-level uncertainty and correction across the many analyses are insufficiently addressed. The pooled voxel null distribution also requires stronger justification.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite extensive documentation: the manuscript shows a blank code-release URL, relies on a proprietary dated GPT-4o endpoint, and omits or leaves unclear some consequential settings such as the keyword-filtering threshold and generation randomness. The full pipeline is also computationally expensive at roughly 83 hours per subject.

The BOLD5000 experiment is useful but does not compare LaVCa with BrainSCUBA or other baselines there, so it demonstrates nonzero transfer rather than preservation of the claimed advantage on an independent dataset.
